rationale: PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait aortic stenosis: its trait_reported/trait_efo are directly aortic stenosis and phenotyping_reported is incident aortic stenosis, whereas PGS005255 is primarily labeled as a related measurement (Mean pressure gradient) with a broader/mixed trait_efo despite sharing the same incident AS endpoint. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, the main differentiators are endpoint fidelity and effect-size evidence; PGS005254 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.64 vs 1.53) and is trained on a larger sample (205,483 vs 98,645) under otherwise identical method (PRS-CS), ancestry (EUR), covariates, and validation size.

PGS005048 and PGS005057 are near-clones: identical endpoint fidelity (Angina pectoris PheCode 411.3; trait_efo angina pectoris; phenotyping_reported Angina pectoris), same study/publication, same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same validation size (n=30,750) and ancestry distribution, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With metrics essentially tied, the only visible differentiators are tiny performance/effect-size edges: PGS005048 has a marginally higher full-model C-index (0.76688 vs 0.76637) and slightly higher OR per SD (1.487 vs 1.479). These differences are small and likely noise, so confidence is low, but they weakly favor PGS005048.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB sparse snpnet framework (same training cohort/size, covariates, variant count=10, ancestry distribution, and validation size), so the main differentiator is endpoint fidelity. PGS001267 targets a direct ankylosing spondylitis case-control style endpoint (phenotyping_reported: "Ankylosing spondylitis"), which better matches the generic target trait than PGS001268’s time-to-event formulation (phenotyping_reported: "TTE ankylosing spondylitis"), a known weaker/packaged endpoint for generic disease risk. Although PGS001268 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.7346/0.1023 vs 0.7265/0.0988), the gap is small and doesn’t outweigh the cleaner endpoint match of PGS001267.

Both candidates are near-clones: same angina pectoris PheCode 411.3 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same method (ldpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distributions, and same validation size (n=30,750). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index is only a weak tie-break. PGS005048 has a trivially higher full-model C-index (0.76688 vs 0.76625) while effect sizes are essentially identical (OR 1.487 vs 1.491), so PGS005048 edges out on the only differentiating metric, but the difference is likely noise → low confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones: same angina pectoris PheCode 411.3 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same publication and cohort context (MVP), same basic covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution and identical validation sample size (n=30,750), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index ~0.766, which is not PRS-comparable). With metrics essentially tied (PGS005057 has a trivially higher full-model C-index, likely noise), the only meaningful differentiator is effect size: PGS005052 shows a slightly higher per-SD OR (1.491 vs 1.479), suggesting marginally stronger PRS signal. Given the tiny differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is low.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_efo=atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported=incident atopic dermatitis), use the same basic covariates, and have identical EUR evaluation size (n=337,910) with only HR(high vs low PRS) reported (no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either). With metrics essentially non-differentiating, structural/model-quality signals dominate: PGS002755 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is generally better suited to polygenic disease risk than PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNP score. The slightly higher HR for PGS002755 (1.249 vs 1.153) also supports stronger discrimination. PGS004587’s listed multi-cohort development is a mild plus, but not enough to outweigh the much stronger method/coverage and effect-size evidence favoring PGS002755.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural and effect-size evidence. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with far broader variant coverage (326,000 vs 858) and shows a slightly stronger risk stratification (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51] vs 1.76 [1.32–2.34] for PGS002739). PGS002739 is evaluated in AFR only and is gene-based/sparse, which is a weaker structural signal for a polygenic disorder absent clearly superior performance. Given similar validation sizes and unknown covariates for both, the broader genome-wide construction plus stronger OR supports PGS002738 as more likely to rank higher overall.

PGS004913 is more endpoint-faithful to the target deployment context: it is explicitly an alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis PRS developed/validated among heavy drinkers, whereas PGS000704 comes from a broad UK Biobank biomarker genetics framework and only reports a covariate-influenced full-model C-index (0.711) plus a modest HR=1.18, with no PRS-only AUC/R². While PGS000704 has a much larger training/validation scale and a stronger genome-wide method/variant count, its performance evidence is not PRS-comparable and likely reflects general biobank modeling rather than a disease-focused cirrhosis risk score. PGS004913, despite smaller samples and also lacking explicit PRS-only AUC, provides more directly PRS-relevant evidence (R²=0.029 and strong top-vs-bottom decile OR=4.4) under basic covariates, making it better-supported for alcoholic liver cirrhosis risk prediction.

PGS004587 is better aligned to the generic target trait “atopic eczema” because it models incident atopic dermatitis (a direct disease endpoint) in a large European evaluation cohort (n=337,910) and reports a PRS effect size (HR high vs low PRS=1.153, 95% CI 1.037–1.282) without relying on family-history/ethnicity packaging. In contrast, PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis) and its only reported discrimination (AUROC=0.93, R²=0.49) appears to be full-model and is paired with parental ethnicity covariates, making the very high metrics non-comparable to PRS-only performance and potentially covariate-driven; it also has much smaller validation (n=676). Neither candidate provides clean PRS-only AUC/R², so endpoint fidelity and comparability favor PGS004587.

PGS000201 has stronger PRS construction support and cleaner evaluation context for the target alcohol dependence spectrum: it uses a genome-wide PRS-CS model with ~1.09M variants and reports an incremental ΔR²=0.01192 with explicit basic covariates, and its phenotyping_reported is DSM-5 alcohol use disorder criteria count (closely aligned to alcohol dependence measurement). In contrast, PGS002739 matches the target label more directly (trait_efo=alcohol dependence) and shows a useful risk stratification OR (top 10% vs rest=1.76), but it is a very sparse 858-variant gene-based score with unknown covariates and AFR-only evaluation, which reduces confidence in general benchmark ranking versus the more standard genome-wide PRS-CS disease-spectrum score.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUC/C-index is not a reliable differentiator—especially since PGS005168 includes CHARGE-AF in covariates, which is explicit clinical risk-calculator packaging and strongly discounts its high full-model C-index (0.8718) as PRS evidence. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), avoiding that leakage concern, and also shows strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.82) with broader evaluation ancestry coverage (multi-ancestry evaluation vs EUR-only for PGS005168). While PGS005168 has a strong HR (1.67) and larger EUR validation n, the CHARGE-AF packaging makes its reported discrimination less comparable, so PGS005313 is better-supported as a standalone AF PRS.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target EFO (alcoholic liver cirrhosis), but PGS000704 has stronger structural support for a standalone PRS: it is a genome-wide snpnet multi-PRS with very large variant count (183,271) and large-scale UKB development (n=223,327) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch), whereas PGS001777 is a 3-variant score with unknown covariates and a much smaller evaluation sample (n=1,390), making its reported full-model AUROC (0.671) hard to interpret for PRS quality. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUC difference (0.711 vs 0.671) is not decisive; the decision is driven by PGS000704’s much stronger methodological/coverage signals and broader evaluation ancestry (EUR+MAE) versus PGS001777’s sparse, potentially less transferable construction despite its high top-vs-bottom OR.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/efo rheumatoid arthritis; phenotyping_reported Seropositive RA), same study/publication, same training cohort (UKB), same training size (n=820), same ancestry distribution and evaluation size (n=90,274), and both report only full-model AUROC/R² (no PRS-only metrics), so metrics are only weakly comparable. Given that, the best differentiator is the within-family empirical performance: PGS004049 shows consistently stronger reported discrimination/effect size than PGS004079 (full-model AUROC 0.728 vs 0.719; R² 0.122 vs 0.113; OR per SD 2.37 vs 2.22; β 0.863 vs 0.798). Variant count differences are modest and cross-method, so they don’t outweigh the stronger observed performance signals for PGS004049.

PGS002738 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is a direct clinical disorder phenotype (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Alcohol use disorder; trait_efo: alcohol dependence), whereas PGS000201 is primarily framed as “Problematic alcohol use” with trait_efo mapped to an alcohol dependence measurement (more proxy/measurement-like despite DSM-5 criteria count). Neither candidate reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be compared on the preferred metrics; in that setting, PGS002738 has stronger disease-focused support signals (multi-cohort development: MVP + UKB) and a substantial risk stratification effect (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96) versus PGS000201’s modest incremental ΔR²=0.01192. PGS000201 does have cleaner/basic covariate disclosure and a larger variant count, but those advantages don’t outweigh PGS002738’s closer disease-endpoint fidelity and stronger effect-size evidence.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to ankylosing spondylitis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and use only basic covariates, so phenotype fidelity and leakage concerns don’t separate them. PGS001267 has cleaner PRS-only metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.7265; PGS-only R2=0.0988), but it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 10-variant snpnet model—an archetype that domain guidance flags as often generalizing poorly. PGS002089, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, is a genome-wide shrinkage score (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (22,026) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (EUR/GME/SAS), which is more consistent with robust external transfer. Given the framework+sparsity warning on PGS001267 versus the stronger structural properties and portability context of PGS002089, PGS002089 is the better-supported pick despite missing directly comparable PRS-only metrics.

PGS002089 is the stronger-supported choice because its endpoint is a direct ankylosing spondylitis diagnosis (phenotyping_reported: "Ankylosing spondylitis") and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with broad variant coverage (22,026 variants), which is structurally more likely to generalize than the very sparse snpnet model in PGS001268 (10 variants) from the known pan-trait "813 traits" framework. Although PGS001268 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (PGS-only AUROC 0.7346; R2 0.10232), it is explicitly time-to-event ("TTE ankylosing spondylitis"), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic disease target, and its sparse framework archetype is a documented portability risk. PGS002089 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 but provides a PRS-comparable partial correlation (partial-r 0.0919) and includes multi-ancestry evaluation (EUR/GME/SAS), supporting transportability; overall the endpoint/method/coverage package is more likely to rank higher externally than the sparse TTE framework score.

PGS004913 has cleaner endpoint fidelity to the target: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis, whereas PGS001777’s phenotyping_reported is “Cirrhosis (males)”, a broader/sex-restricted endpoint that is less directly aligned to alcoholic liver cirrhosis. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS001777’s full-model AUROC=0.671 is not a comparable PRS metric and is further hard to interpret with covariates listed as unknown; by contrast PGS004913 discloses basic covariates (age, sex, PCs) and reports a modest R²=0.029 plus an OR top vs bottom deciles=4.4, providing more interpretable PRS-focused evidence without obvious clinical-risk packaging. Both are EUR-only, but overall PGS004913 is better-supported on phenotype alignment and comparability.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and EUR-only evaluation. However, PGS001784 comes from a clear portability/framework paper (“Global Biobank analyses… across diverse cohorts”), which domain guidance flags as systematically underperforming disease-focused models unless it has clearly superior PRS-comparable evidence. While PGS001784 reports a PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke R2 covariates-regressed-out = 0.014661, below the h2_liability ceiling 0.02 and thus plausible), its very high AUROC (0.868) is likely largely covariate-driven given the explicit age/sex/PC covariates and is not a PRS-only AUROC. PGS003972 is from a disease-focused AAA GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet, multi-cohort consortium-style development) using PRS-CS with higher variant count (1.12M vs 0.91M), which is a stronger archetype for external performance despite lacking PRS-only metrics and having unknown covariates; its reported AUROC (0.69) is also full-model and not directly comparable. Given the strong penalty for framework-origin scores and the disease-focused multi-cohort context plus slightly stronger structural properties, PGS003972 is the better-supported choice overall.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target disease endpoint: its trait_reported/trait_efo are directly aortic stenosis and phenotyping is incident aortic stenosis cases, whereas PGS005255 is labeled as a valve-function measurement (mean pressure gradient) with a mixed trait_efo (aortic stenosis, aortic measurement), creating weaker endpoint fidelity despite also mentioning incident aortic stenosis in phenotyping. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size and design signals: PGS005252 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255), suggesting stronger standalone PRS discrimination. Although PGS005252 reports only a full-model C-index 0.87 with heavy clinical covariates (making that metric non-comparable), PGS005255 provides no comparable discrimination metric either, and its lighter covariate set does not compensate for the weaker endpoint labeling and smaller HR. Ancestry is identical (EUR-only) and validation sizes are not decisive.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model discrimination is not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS005168’s reported C-index 0.8718 is heavily discounted because its covariates explicitly include the CHARGE-AF clinical risk calculator (risk-wrapper packaging), making the full-model metric likely covariate-driven and less informative about standalone PRS quality. In contrast, PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that leakage concern, and it shows strong PRS signal via effect size (OR≈1.94 per SD) with a large, disease-focused cross-ancestry GWAS development context. Despite PGS005168 having a more modern shrinkage method and many more variants, the CHARGE-AF packaging makes its visible performance evidence less trustworthy for benchmarking standalone PRS, so PGS002814 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates are essentially matched on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo = rheumatoid arthritis; phenotyping_reported = Seropositive RA), covariates (0), training cohort (UKB), ancestry distribution, and validation size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not directly comparable PRS metrics). Given this near-clone setup, the differentiators are the within-study empirical performance and structural signals: PGS004163 shows higher reported AUROC (0.7469 vs 0.7193), higher R² (0.1376 vs 0.1129), and stronger effect sizes (OR 2.46 vs 2.22; β 0.901 vs 0.798) than PGS004079, and it is an ensemble MultiPRS method with a larger variant set (778,275 vs 402,214), which is a positive structural signal when other fields are aligned. Therefore PGS004163 is better-supported than PGS004079 on the visible evidence.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo aortic stenosis; incident aortic stenosis phenotyping) and both are EUR-only in development/evaluation with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so we must lean on effect-size evidence and study design signals rather than full-model discrimination. PGS005254 is better-supported by a much larger training sample (n=205,483 vs n=47,691 for PGS005252) and a clean PRS-associated effect size with CI (HR=1.64, 1.50–1.78), while PGS005252’s headline C-index=0.87 is a full-model metric paired with a very heavy clinical covariate set (multiple comorbidities and BMI/smoking/renal failure), making it likely covariate-driven and not comparable as PRS evidence. Although PGS005252 reports a higher HR (1.92), the lack of CI plus the covariate-heavy packaging and reliance on full-model C-index reduce confidence that it reflects stronger standalone PRS performance than the larger, more cleanly adjusted PGS005254.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match abdominal aortic aneurysm) and both are evaluated in EUR. However, PGS001784 comes from a clear portability/framework archetype (“Global Biobank analyses provide lessons…”) and uses a heavier covariate set (age/sex interactions + 20 PCs), with only modest PRS-comparable signal (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.014661, below the ~0.02 liability h2 ceiling but not especially strong). PGS003973 is from a disease-focused AAA GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet, AAA-specific loci/PCSK9 focus) with a large, consortium-like development cohort list and cleaner/basic covariates (age, age^2, sex), plus a more genome-wide score (1,118,997 vs 911,440 variants). Although PGS003973 lacks explicit PRS-only R2/AUC (only a full-model C-index), the disease-focused study archetype + cleaner covariate design and slightly stronger structural properties make it more likely to transfer well than the framework-derived PGS001784.

PGS002727 is from a disease-focused pediatric asthma study (“Multiancestral polygenic risk score for pediatric asthma”) using a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large genome-wide coverage (985,837 variants) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.57), plus broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS). In contrast, PGS001344 comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank framework (“across 813 traits”), uses a very sparse snpnet model (6,139 variants) that domain guidance flags as often less transferable, even though it provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6457; R2=0.0597) with basic covariates. Given the framework penalty and structural/transportability advantages of the disease-focused, genome-wide multi-ancestry score, PGS002727 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarking despite lacking explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.78 in PGS005313 vs 0.74 in PGS002814) are only weakly informative. PGS005313 is better-supported structurally and for likely external performance: it uses a genome-wide cross-ancestry shrinkage approach (PRS-CSx) with far more variants (1,271,239 vs 4,520 for P+T in PGS002814), and it is developed/validated in a broader multi-ancestry context (GWAS includes AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS and evaluation spans multiple ancestries) rather than being trained in MAE and evaluated only in EAS for PGS002814. Covariates are similarly light (age/sex; PGS002814 adds PCs), and both report strong per-SD ORs, with PGS005313’s OR=1.82 comparable to PGS002814’s OR≈1.94. Given the lack of PRS-only metrics, the method/coverage and broader transportability evidence favor PGS005313.

PGS002727 is better supported for the target asthma endpoint because it is from a disease-focused pediatric asthma study with explicit endpoint specificity (phenotyping_reported: Pediatric asthma) and shows strong PRS signal via an OR=1.57 per SD, plus broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS each 20%) and very large overall validation (n=391,820). In contrast, PGS001782 comes from a known portability/framework-style paper (“Global Biobank analyses…”) and is evaluated only in EUR; while it reports a clean PRS-comparable Nagelkerke R2=0.048844 (below the asthma h2_liability ceiling), that single-metric advantage is modest and sits in a framework context that domain guidance says typically underperforms disease-focused models unless it has clearly superior endpoint+metric evidence. Both have similar full-model AUROC (~0.66), but PGS002727’s endpoint focus and multi-ancestry evaluation outweigh PGS001782’s modest PRS-only R2 edge.

PGS001782 is better-supported for likely external benchmark performance because it comes from a global multi-biobank PRS development context (many training/development cohorts; multi-ancestry GWAS) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with very large variant coverage (884,043), which is structurally favored for a polygenic disease like asthma. Its reported PRS-comparable metric is a covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.048844, which is plausible under the asthma heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.1515). PGS001344, while having slightly higher PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.64568; R2=0.05973) and larger validation n, is explicitly from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”, snpnet, 6,139 variants), a study archetype that domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer than multi-cohort disease-oriented scores; its modest metric edge is not enough to outweigh that framework+sparse-method penalty.

Both candidates are near-clones for abdominal aortic aneurysm (same trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported, same PRS-CS method, same 1,118,997 variants, same GWAS ancestry mix and EUR-only evaluation), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model metrics must be discounted as non-comparable PRS evidence. Given that, PGS003973 has cleaner/transparent basic covariates (Age, Age^2, Sex) whereas PGS003972 lists covariates as Unknown, lowering comparability. The much higher reported full-model C-index (0.882 vs 0.69 AUROC) is not decisive but is at least consistent with a well-specified demographic-adjusted model in PGS003973; other differences (record_count, small validation N difference, extra cohorts listed in PGS003972) are weak signals. Overall, PGS003973 is better-supported on covariate clarity with otherwise equivalent endpoint fidelity and study family.

PGS002755 is better supported as a standalone PRS for the target atopic eczema because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and is evaluated at large scale in EUR (n=337,910) with an endpoint closely matching the target (incident atopic dermatitis). It also provides a PRS-linked effect size (HR high vs low PRS = 1.249), giving at least some PRS-specific signal without relying on a covariate-inflated AUROC. In contrast, PGS001773 targets a narrower phenotype (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis) and is a very sparse 25-variant score; its headline AUROC/R² (0.93/0.49) are full-model/non-PRS-only and are likely dominated by covariates (including parental ethnicity), making the performance evidence non-comparable and potentially inflated relative to the trait heritability ceiling. Thus, despite PGS002755 lacking PRS-only AUC/R², its endpoint fidelity plus stronger structural PRS properties make it more likely to transfer well.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/efo = rheumatoid arthritis; phenotyping_reported = Seropositive RA), covariates (0), training cohort (UKB), training size (n=820), ancestry distribution, and validation size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not ideal for PRS comparison). Given this tie on design/phenotype, PGS004163 has the more supportive performance/effect-size signals in the selected European validation record (higher full-model AUROC 0.7469 vs 0.7283; higher R² 0.1376 vs 0.1220; slightly higher OR per SD 2.46 vs 2.37) and also uses an ensemble-style method (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) which is structurally favored over a single-method score (LDpred2.CV) when other fields are effectively identical.

PGS001263 is a direct endpoint match to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”), whereas PGS002050 is a combined phenotype (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”), which is less specific to atrial flutter alone. PGS001263 also provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R2=0.025), and the PGS-only R2 is plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0157) as a sanity check signal rather than an obvious inflation. PGS002050 has a method/structure advantage (LDpred2 with ~555k variants vs sparse 2,087 SNPs) and similar multi-ancestry evaluation framing, but it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 and reports only partial-r, making its expected standalone PRS discrimination for atrial flutter harder to benchmark and less directly supported for this specific target.

PGS000327 is clearly endpoint-faithful to the target: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to autism spectrum disorder, and it comes from a disease-focused ASD GWAS meta-analysis context with broad ASD cohorts listed. It also provides stronger PRS-relevant evidence (OR per SD = 1.33 with tight CI) and a higher reported R² (0.0245, albeit as full-model/unspecified) than PGS002790’s much smaller partial R² (0.00546). In contrast, PGS002790 has an explicit phenotype mismatch in phenotyping_reported (“Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)”), unclear training sample size (N/A), and looks more like a cross-trait/behavioral analysis despite the ASD label, making its performance less directly attributable to ASD risk prediction.

PGS001263 is a tighter endpoint match to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all specifically “Atrial flutter”), whereas PGS001841 uses a combined endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”), which is a fidelity dilution for an atrial-flutter-only benchmark. PGS001263 also provides clean PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R2=0.025), and the PRS-only R2 is plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0157), giving interpretable standalone-PRS evidence; PGS001841 reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.1026) and no PRS-only AUROC/R2, making cross-model performance comparison weaker. Both are UKB-derived framework/portability-style scores with broadly similar basic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation, so the decision is driven mainly by PGS001263’s exact phenotype alignment plus directly comparable PRS-only performance reporting.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same publication/family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and essentially identical full-model AUROC (0.632 with identical CI). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC cannot separate them as a standalone PRS metric. With endpoints and context tied, the only visible performance separation is slightly stronger PRS signal for PGS000454: marginally higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0489 vs 0.0487) and higher top-1% vs rest OR (3.79 vs 3.61). Given the tiny differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, the win is weakly supported, hence low confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training size, and ancestry distribution/evaluation context; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, and both have essentially identical partial-r (0.1034 for PGS002050 vs 0.1026 for PGS001841). With metrics and design effectively tied, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002050 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (554,908 vs 3,980), which is generally the stronger choice for a polygenic disease endpoint when other evidence is indistinguishable. PGS001841’s sparse penalized regression with a much smaller SNP set offers no compensating performance advantage here.

Both candidates are near-clones: same breast cancer endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication, same variant count (1,041,298), same training cohort (UKB) and training N (12,483), same ancestry distribution, same stated covariates (0), and same validation N (48,968). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC/R² are not strong differentiators and are essentially identical (0.65979 vs 0.65976; R² 0.07392 vs 0.07359), as are effect sizes (OR per SD ~1.81 for both). With no meaningful empirical separation, I apply the weak prior toward candidate_a and select PGS004040 over PGS004025.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait “bipolar disorder” at the concept level (trait_reported/trait_efo both bipolar disorder), whereas PGS002787 is explicitly bipolar I disorder (a subtype) and thus slightly less endpoint-aligned for a broad bipolar disorder target. Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), have similar variant counts and EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; the only metric difference is a tiny full-model partial R² edge for PGS002787 (0.00275 vs 0.00251) which is not a robust differentiator and is not PRS-only. Given near-tie on design/metrics and the stronger trait alignment, PGS002786 narrowly wins.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (basal cell carcinoma), same method (GWAS Hits), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC reported with basic covariates). With endpoint fidelity and study context indistinguishable, the only differentiators are small, likely-noise metric/structure differences: PGS000452 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.632 vs 0.630) and higher pseudo-R² (0.0487 vs 0.0456), while PGS000456 has a higher top-1% OR (3.95 vs 3.61) and 2 more variants (30 vs 28). Given the guidance that small full-model AUROC differences are weak and that effect-size evidence can break ties, this is essentially a toss-up; I pick PGS000452 on the slightly stronger overall discrimination summary (AUROC and pseudo-R²) under identical covariates.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all basal cell carcinoma), same EUR-only ancestry across GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not PRS-comparable). With metrics essentially tied (full-model AUROC 0.632 for PGS000454 vs 0.630 for PGS000456; pseudo-R² 0.0489 vs 0.0456; per-SD OR 1.661 vs 1.633), PGS000454 has a slight edge on the available discrimination/effect-size signals, while PGS000456’s only advantage is a marginally higher top-1% OR and slightly more variants. Given the tiny differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is low.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to celiac disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not cleanly comparable PRS metrics. With metrics largely non-discriminating, structural signals favor PGS000040: it uses a genome-wide statistical learning approach (SparSNP) with a larger variant set (228 vs 53 for PGS000316’s log-additive GRS), which is more likely to capture polygenic signal. The small full-model AUROC difference (0.90 vs 0.879) is minor and both have unknown covariates, but it is at least directionally consistent with PGS000040. PGS000316’s much larger validation N is a weak tie-breaker and doesn’t outweigh the method/variant-count advantage for PGS000040.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Breast cancer/breast carcinoma), study context (same publication), ancestry distribution (same GWAS/DEV/EVAL mix), covariates (0), training cohort (UKB) and training/validation sizes. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the best available differentiators are the within-family full-model metrics/effect sizes and structural signals: PGS004153 shows consistently slightly stronger reported performance and effect size than PGS004025 (AUROC 0.6625 vs 0.6598; R² 0.0764 vs 0.0736; OR per SD 1.826 vs 1.806), and also has a modestly higher variant count (1,133,268 vs 1,041,298). Given otherwise identical design, these small but consistent advantages favor PGS004153.

PGS001033 has the closest endpoint alignment to the target: its trait_efo is exactly "blood coagulation disease" and phenotyping is explicitly "TTE other coagulation defects", whereas PGS001826 targets a much narrower congenital clotting-factor deficiency subtype (vitamin K–dependent factors / factor VII) rather than the broader coagulation-disease umbrella. PGS001033 also provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.634 and PGS-only R2 0.0578) under basic covariates, while PGS001826 reports only a modest partial correlation (0.0562) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, leaving weaker directly comparable evidence. Although both are UKB framework-style scores (portability/pan-trait) and PGS001826 uses more variants (45 vs 1), the combination of exact target EFO mapping plus explicit PRS-only metrics makes PGS001033 better-supported overall for the benchmark setting.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Breast cancer/breast carcinoma), study context (same publication), training (UKB; n=12,483), evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS), covariates (0), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only a weak differentiator). Given this, the best available separation is the within-family empirical performance/effect-size edge and structural signals: PGS004153 shows slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6625 vs 0.6598), higher R² (0.0764 vs 0.0739), and marginally stronger OR per SD (1.826 vs 1.809), and it also has a slightly higher variant count (1,133,268 vs 1,041,298). With no other meaningful differences, these consistent small advantages favor PGS004153 over PGS004040.

PGS002032 has cleaner endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both specifically "Disorders of bilirubin excretion" mapped to bilirubin metabolism disease), whereas PGS000924 is a broader composite and explicitly time-to-event ("disorders of porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism (TTE)") spanning two EFO traits, which is a phenotype/endpoint mismatch risk for a generic bilirubin-metabolism-disease target. Although PGS000924 reports strong-looking PRS-only AUROC/R2, those metrics are from a pan-trait UKB sparse snpnet framework with only 5 variants and an R2 (0.218) that exceeds the provided local heritability ceiling (~0.089), making the reported PRS-only performance suspect/non-comparable. PGS002032 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 but comes from a portability evaluation with multi-ancestry EVAL and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with many variants (19,768), and its partial-r (0.0716) is at least consistent with the heritability ceiling, making it the better-supported and more likely-to-transfer choice here.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (Disorders of bilirubin excretion), same UKB portability publication, same training size (n=391,124), same covariates, same ancestry distribution, same validation size (n=19,924), and essentially identical PRS-comparable performance evidence (partial-r=0.0716 for PGS002032 vs 0.0716 for PGS001824). With metrics not differentiating, structural signals dominate: PGS002032 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (19,768) versus PGS001824’s very sparse penalized regression score (22 variants), which is a warning sign for capturing polygenic signal in this framework setting. Therefore PGS002032 is better-supported to rank higher externally, though confidence is only moderate because the observed partial-r is the same in the selected record.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002788 targets bipolar II disorder (a subtype mismatch for a generic bipolar disorder benchmark). Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), have similar variant counts, identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical covariates (age, PCs1-3), and the same validation sample size (n=2,524), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—only small partial R² values tied to non-disease phenotypes. Given near-identical support otherwise, endpoint fidelity breaks the tie in favor of PGS002786; confidence is low because both have weak/indirect phenotyping_reported fields and only full-model partial R² evidence.

PGS004546 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target trait (ICD10 K80 cholelithiasis in both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported, trait_efo exactly cholelithiasis), whereas PGS002072 uses a broader combined endpoint ("Cholelithiasis and cholecystitis"; trait_efo includes both), which is a mild mismatch for a pure cholelithiasis target. Neither candidate reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so performance can’t separate them; however PGS004546 provides a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.30) as direct PRS signal evidence, while PGS002072 only reports a modest partial correlation (partial-r=0.098) that is harder to interpret as standalone discrimination. PGS002072’s multi-ancestry evaluation breadth is a plus, but it comes from a portability-style paper and does not outweigh PGS004546’s cleaner phenotype alignment plus effect-size evidence for this specific target.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo cervical carcinoma). However, PGS003428 is from a disease-focused cervical phenotypes GWAS meta-analysis/risk stratification study with multi-cohort development (EB, FinnGen, KP, UKB) and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred; 2,894,555 variants), which is structurally and archetypically more likely to transfer than the pan-trait UKB sparse framework score PGS001299 ("across 813 traits"; snpnet; only 24 variants). While PGS001299 reports PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.552/0.0026), those are weak and come from the known underperforming pan-trait sparse framework archetype; its high full-model AUROC is largely covariate-driven and not decisive. PGS003428 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 but provides an effect-size signal (HR 1.33) with basic covariates (age, smoking) and large EUR evaluation, making it better-supported overall despite missing PRS-only metrics.

PGS001301 has directly comparable PRS-only performance reported (PGS AUROC no covariates 0.82867; PGS R2 no covariates 0.14224) with explicit basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and its PRS-only R2 is below the celiac disease liability h2 ceiling provided, making the metric package interpretable. PGS000316 is more endpoint-faithful (pure “Coeliac disease” vs the broader “Malabsorption/coeliac disease”) and is disease-focused, but it lacks any PRS-only AUC/R2 and only reports a high full-model AUROC (0.879) with unknown covariates, which is not a valid substitute for PRS discrimination and could be covariate-driven. Given the benchmark goal of predicting standalone PRS performance, the cleaner PRS-only metric evidence in PGS001301 outweighs its framework-paper penalty and slightly broader phenotype label.

PGS001824 has cleaner endpoint fidelity to the target: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are directly "Disorders of bilirubin excretion" mapped to bilirubin metabolism disease, whereas PGS000924 is a mixed endpoint (porphyrin + bilirubin) and explicitly time-to-event, which is a weaker match for a generic disease target. Although PGS000924 reports strong-looking PRS-only AUROC/R2, its PRS-only R2 (0.218) exceeds the provided local heritability ceiling for bilirubin (~0.089), making the metric suspect/non-comparable on the visible evidence; PGS001824’s partial-r is modest but at least not heritability-incoherent. Both are UKB framework-style scores with basic covariates and similar ancestry evaluation patterns, so phenotype alignment and metric sanity-check drive the decision.

PGS001033 is the better-supported match to the target trait because its trait_efo is exactly "blood coagulation disease" and its phenotyping_reported is a directly aligned coagulation-defect endpoint (albeit time-to-event). It also reports clean PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.634 and PGS-only R²=0.0578) under basic covariates, giving direct evidence of standalone PRS signal. In contrast, PGS002034 targets a much narrower congenital clotting-factor deficiency subtype (vitamin K–dependent factor deficiency / factor VII-related), which is a partial mismatch to the broad target "blood coagulation disease", and it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a partial correlation is shown), making its predictive support less directly comparable despite a larger variant count and similar UKB-based design.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same publication, same method (SDPR), similar genome-wide variant counts (~935k), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same basic covariates (age, PCs1-3), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a small full-model/partial R² is shown, so metrics are weakly comparable). With endpoint fidelity otherwise similarly imperfect for the target “bipolar disorder” (each is a subtype: bipolar I vs bipolar II, and phenotyping_reported fields look behavior-proxy rather than direct diagnosis), the only consistent differentiators are slightly higher reported partial R² (0.00307 vs 0.00275) and slightly larger validation N (2,524 vs 2,198) for PGS002788. These are small differences, hence low confidence, but they favor PGS002788 over PGS002787.

PGS002237 has tighter endpoint fidelity via an explicit CKD definition (eGFR <45 ml/min per 1.73 m2; stage 3+), and—critically—shows broader external evaluation across multiple ancestries (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE) rather than being restricted to a single ancestry context. Both candidates only report full-model AUROC (no PRS-only AUC/R2), so PGS005090’s higher AUROC=0.90 is not a reliable PRS-comparable advantage, especially given different covariate sets. While PGS005090 uses a structurally stronger method (PRS-CS) and has large AFR evaluation, it lacks training sample size metadata (N/A) and is single-ancestry GWAS/EVAL, making it less supported for general CKD benchmarking than the multi-ancestry, explicitly phenotyped PGS002237.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training size, and evaluation ancestry/validation N, and they show essentially identical PRS-comparable performance evidence (partial-r 0.0563 for PGS002034 vs 0.0562 for PGS001826 with overlapping CIs). With metrics unable to differentiate, structural signals become the tie-break: PGS002034 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (32,552 variants) versus the very sparse penalized regression score (45 variants) in PGS001826, which is a warning sign for capturing polygenic signal in general. Therefore PGS002034 is better-supported to rank higher, though confidence is only moderate because the observed performance is effectively tied.

PGS004476 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target trait cholelithiasis: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly ICD10 K80 (Cholelithiasis) with trait_efo=cholelithiasis, whereas PGS002072 uses a broader composite endpoint ("Cholelithiasis and cholecystitis") and even maps trait_efo to "Cholecystitis, cholelithiasis", introducing phenotype heterogeneity. Neither candidate reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so performance metrics do not differentiate; in that setting, PGS004476’s much larger genome-wide variant set (1,059,939 vs 428,587; both LDpred2-family) plus a moderate per-SD OR (1.22) provides some direct PRS signal, while PGS002072’s partial-r=0.098 is hard to compare and comes from a known portability-style framework paper. Although PGS002072 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and explicit basic covariates, the framework/portability archetype and less specific endpoint make it less likely to rank highest for a cholelithiasis benchmark than the more endpoint-faithful PGS004476.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (ICD10 K80 cholelithiasis), ancestry (EUR-only dev/eval), cohorts (UKB), training size (n=174,489) and validation size (n=56,192), and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR per SD). With metrics absent, the main differentiators are structural/modeling signals and effect size. PGS004546 uses an aggregated/meta-PRS approach (RFDiseasemetaPRS), which is a positive structural signal versus the single-score LDpred2 model in PGS004476, and it also shows a stronger per-SD OR (1.299 vs 1.219), suggesting better standalone discrimination. Given otherwise identical context and unknown covariates for both, PGS004546 is better-supported.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident cervical cancer; EUR evaluation). However, PGS003428 is from a cervical-phenotype GWAS meta-analysis/risk stratification study and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred) with very large variant coverage (2,894,555), which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than PGS000073’s 10 genome-wide significant SNPs from a cross-cancer evaluation paper. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC/C-index for PGS000073 (≈0.745–0.75) is not a reliable PRS discriminator, especially given its much heavier covariate set (PCs, parity, oral contraceptive use, pack-years) versus PGS003428’s lighter covariates (age, smoking). With comparable endpoint fidelity and no clean PRS-only metrics, the disease-focused meta-analysis context + genome-wide method/coverage favors PGS003428 despite its lower full-model C-index (0.613).

PGS002237 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint is more specific and clinically anchored to CKD severity (stage 3+; eGFR <45), and it comes from a CKD-focused cross-ancestry prediction study with explicit multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE), which is supportive of transportability. Although its only visible AUROC (0.78) is a full-model metric with substantial clinical covariates (hypertension, diabetes, BMI, medication use), it also reports a relatively strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.47), providing some PRS signal evidence. In contrast, PGS004158 is from a methods/biobank benchmarking paper, uses a broader composite phenotype (“CKD or dialysis”), and while it has no covariates (cleaner comparability), its reported discrimination is much weaker (AUROC ~0.592; OR ~1.39) and offers no PRS-only metrics either—making it less likely to rank highly on external CKD benchmarks despite the larger validation sample.

Both candidates align to the target (trait_efo cervical carcinoma). PGS001299 is a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse snpnet score (“across 813 traits”) with explicit PRS-only metrics, but those are very weak for cervical cancer (PGS-only AUROC 0.552, PGS-only R2 0.00263) and its apparent full-model AUROC (0.768) is largely covariate-driven (incremental AUROC only 0.00676). PGS000073 comes from a cancer-focused cross-cancer evaluation study with an incident cervical cancer endpoint and provides an effect-size signal (HR 1.22 per SD) plus time-to-event discrimination (C-index 0.75) in a large evaluation cohort; despite lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, it avoids the known underperformance pattern of pan-trait sparse UKB framework scores and has more disease-relevant evaluation context. Net: PGS000073 is better-supported for likely external performance than the very low-signal PRS-only metrics of PGS001299.

PGS000040 is a disease-focused coeliac disease model with direct endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Coeliac disease”) and a high reported AUROC (0.9) in its validation context, whereas PGS001301 comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank framework (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer despite clean PRS-only metrics. Although PGS001301 reports explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.8287/0.1422) with only basic covariates and larger training/validation, its phenotype label is broader (“Malabsorption/coeliac disease”) and its framework archetype is a strong negative signal relative to a targeted disease study. PGS000040 lacks PRS-only metrics (its 0.9 AUROC may be full-model), lowering certainty, but the combination of tighter endpoint specificity and non-framework study design makes it more likely to rank higher in an external benchmark for celiac disease.

PGS004536 has tighter endpoint fidelity to COPD via explicit ICD-10 J44 phenotyping/trait_reported and provides a strong PRS-discrimination proxy (OR per SD = 1.49, near the ≥1.5 “strong” guideline), plus a multi-score aggregation structure (risk-factor metaPRS + disease PRS) and larger validation (56,192 EUR). PGS002062 comes from a UKB portability framework paper with a broader/less specific phenotype label (“Chronic airway obstruction”) and only a weak PRS-comparable signal (partial-r = 0.047), despite broader multi-ancestry evaluation and larger training N. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the stronger effect-size evidence and more diagnosis-anchored endpoint make PGS004536 more likely to rank higher.

PGS004158 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait “chronic kidney disease” because its endpoint is broader and closer to the umbrella CKD concept (phenotyping_reported: “Chronic kidney disease or dialysis”) and it is evaluated across more than one ancestry group (EVAL: EUR and SAS), which is a positive transportability signal versus PGS005090 being AFR-only in both GWAS and evaluation. While PGS005090 reports much higher full-model AUROC/R² (0.9/0.1), those are not PRS-only metrics and are paired with explicit clinical covariates (age, sex, diabetes, PCs), making the apparent performance likely covariate-inflated and not directly comparable; its R²=0.1 also looks high relative to the provided CKD heritability ceiling (EUR h2_obs≈0.012), further reducing trust in that metric as PRS signal. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R², so the decision falls back to endpoint fidelity and robustness/transportability, where PGS004158 has the clearer advantage.

PGS004536 is the better-supported COPD PRS because it shows stronger PRS-specific signal and a more disease-focused construction: it reports an OR=1.49 per SD (a strong effect-size indicator for PRS discrimination) and uses an explicit multi-score aggregation approach (RFDiseasemetaPRS integrating risk-factor PRS with disease PRS), with large training (n=174,489) and large EUR validation (n=56,192) on an ICD-10 J44 COPD endpoint. In contrast, PGS001783 comes from a portability/framework-style global biobank paper and, while it provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.038, below the h2_liability ceiling 0.0388), it lacks training N and its reported AUROC=0.74 is full-model with covariates (age/sex/PCs) rather than PRS-only; the PRS-only R2 is only modest. Both are endpoint-aligned to COPD, but the stronger effect-size evidence and disease/meta-PRS structure favor PGS004536.

Both candidates are near-clones (same CAD endpoint/phenotyping, same LDpred2 method, same variant count, same training N and validation N, and similarly clean basic covariates), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. The main differentiator is performance evidence: PGS003725 shows stronger effect-size support (OR per SD 2.14 and HR 1.75) versus PGS003726 reporting only a slightly lower HR 1.73 with no OR, giving PGS003725 a more compelling and better-supported discrimination signal. Differences in ancestry_distribution and training cohort list are secondary here and don’t outweigh the stronger effect-size package in PGS003725.

PGS001783 is the better-supported COPD score because it has exact endpoint fidelity (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both “Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease”) and provides a clean PRS-comparable metric: Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2 = 0.038092, which is plausible relative to the provided liability h2 ceiling (~0.0388). In contrast, PGS002062 comes from a UKB portability framework study and uses a less direct phenotype label (“Chronic airway obstruction”); it reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.047) rather than a directly comparable PRS-only R2/AUC, making performance support weaker for benchmarking. Although PGS002062 has larger training/validation and multi-ancestry evaluation, the framework archetype plus weaker comparable metrics and slightly looser endpoint wording make it less likely to rank higher than the more endpoint-faithful model with an explicit PRS-only R2.

Both candidates are near-clones (same CAD endpoint/phenotyping, same LDpred2 method, same training n=116,649, same validation size n=308,264, and similarly basic covariates), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on structural and effect-size evidence. PGS003726 has a higher per-SD effect size (HR 1.73 vs 1.67 for PGS003727) and a modestly larger variant count (1,296,172 vs 1,125,113), both supportive of stronger standalone PRS signal within the same method/publication family. Although PGS003727 uses EUR-only GWAS and has more performance records, those are weak differentiators here given identical endpoint and missing comparable metrics.

ontology: congenital vitamin k-dependent coagulation factors deficiency
rationale: Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training size, and evaluation ancestry/validation N; and they show essentially identical partial-r performance (0.0563 vs 0.0562). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes to separate them, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002034 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (32,552 variants) versus PGS001826’s very sparse penalized regression score (45 variants). Given the same endpoint and comparable observed performance, the higher-coverage shrinkage model is better-supported to capture polygenic signal and thus more likely to rank higher externally.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate cirrhosis). However, PGS004621 is a disease-focused, modern genome-wide PRS-CS model with very large genome-wide coverage (1,089,806 variants) and a large European evaluation sample (n=1,153,995) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than PGS000726’s 12-variant genome-wide-significant score. While neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R2, PGS004621 at least reports a per-SD OR of 1.42 (moderate signal) and its reported AUROC=0.68 is explicitly a full-model metric (not over-interpreted), whereas PGS000726 lacks AUC/R2 entirely and relies mainly on a top-vs-bottom quintile OR (2.26) that is less directly comparable across studies. Overall, the combination of genome-wide method/variant coverage and large evaluation support favors PGS004621 over the sparse-hit model PGS000726.

PGS001331 is the better-supported choice for generic Crohn’s disease risk: it matches the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are plain Crohn’s disease), whereas PGS001330 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) formulation, which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease target. Both are from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework with identical training cohort/size, covariates, and validation size, so performance and structure are the main differentiators; PGS001331 has slightly stronger PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.579 vs 0.576; PGS-only R² 0.00677 vs 0.00621) and more variants (257 vs 220). Both R² values are well below the Crohn’s heritability ceiling, so the small metric edge for PGS001331 is credible.

Both candidates match the target trait well (all-cause dementia; EFO dementia), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS004281 (0.819 vs 0.761) is not a reliable standalone PRS differentiator. PGS005170 is better-supported structurally and for external transfer: it is an explicit multi-score integrative/ensemble PRS (24 component PRSs; 1.32M variants) with multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR) and provides an HR per SD (1.25, moderate signal), whereas PGS004281 is a very sparse 110-variant single-UKB GenoBoost score evaluated only in EUR with no effect-size evidence. Given domain guidance favoring disease-focused, externally oriented multi-cohort/robustness signals and multi-score aggregation when PRS-only metrics are absent, PGS005170 is more likely to generalize and rank higher in an external benchmark than the single-biobank sparse alternative.

PGS000726 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are generic “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver”, whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to “Alcoholic cirrhosis” (trait_efo: alcoholic liver cirrhosis), a subtype mismatch for a broad cirrhosis target. PGS000726 also comes from a disease-focused cirrhosis GWAS/meta-style study with multiple development cohorts (ACG, ARIC, BBJ, BioVU, FinnGen, PHB, UKB) and shows a stronger PRS effect-size signal (OR per SD 1.32; top-vs-bottom quintile OR 2.26) than PGS000704’s HR 1.18. PGS000704’s only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index 0.711 (not PRS-only) from a biomarker-focused UKB paper, so it is less informative for standalone PRS ranking and more likely to be framework-like/less endpoint-focused than PGS000726.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target/endpoint (All-cause dementia; EFO dementia), same method (GenoBoost), same training cohort and size (UKB; n=269,710), same EUR-only dev/eval ancestry, same covariates (age, sex, PC1-10), and same validation size (n=67,428). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC (~0.819) is not a reliable PRS comparator and the tiny AUROC/R2 differences between them are essentially noise. With performance and design indistinguishable, the only meaningful structural differentiator is variants_number: PGS004281 uses more variants (110 vs 50), which is a modest within-method advantage and thus slightly better-supported for capturing polygenic signal.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait (Major Depressive Disorder, lifetime), same EFO (major depressive disorder), same phenotyping_reported (Major depressive disorder), same method (PRSice-2), same variant count (4,786,322), same training cohort (UKB) and training N (67,164), same covariates (PCs 1–10), and same multi-ancestry evaluation distribution with the selected validation ancestry being European and the same validation sample size (42,250). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; both only show a full-model R², which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric. With everything else effectively identical, the only visible differentiator is a trivially higher reported R² for PGS003578 (0.0257 vs 0.0254 for PGS003580), so PGS003578 is selected, but the evidence gap is minimal.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to Crohn’s disease) and similarly basic covariates. However, PGS001331 is explicitly a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-framework score ("across 813 traits"; snpnet with only 257 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically underperforming in external validation despite clean metadata; its PRS-only metrics are also weak (PGS-only AUROC 0.579, R2 0.00677). PGS004254, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC 0.72), is structurally a genome-wide shrinkage PRS (LDpred2-auto; 744,682 variants) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR 2.18), which is meaningful evidence of PRS discriminative power and more consistent with stronger real-world performance than the sparse framework score. Overall, the method/variant-count plus strong OR outweigh PGS001331’s modest PRS-only AUROC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all corneal dystrophy), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (n=19,321), so the decision rests on comparative PRS signal and structural properties. Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait (Major Depressive Disorder, lifetime), same EFO mapping, same phenotyping_reported, same method (PRSice-2), same training cohort (UKB), same training N (67,164), same covariates (PCs 1–10), same multi-ancestry evaluation mix and validation N (42,250), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a full-model/unspecified R²). PGS004614 is the better-supported same-trait PRS: it is clearly disease-focused (publication explicitly on diverticular disease risk variants) with direct phenotype alignment (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Diverticular disease”) and uses a strong genome-wide shrinkage method (SBayesR). Although it only reports a full-model AUROC (0.76) that is likely inflated by explicit family history covariate inclusion (so not PRS-comparable), PGS004544 provides even less directly comparable performance evidence (no AUC/R2 at all, only a moderate OR=1.32) and comes from a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framework paper, which is a packaging signal and less reliably transferable than a direct disease PRS. PGS004614 also shows some multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/SAS) whereas PGS004544 is EUR-only evaluation.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (lifetime MDD), same method (PRSice-2), same training cohort and size (UKB; n=67,164), same covariates (PCs 1-10), same multi-ancestry evaluation mix and validation N (n=42,250), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model R² is shown). PGS004951 is better supported for the target trait (dilated cardiomyopathy) because its endpoint is the direct clinical DCM phenotype (“Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy”), whereas PGS004947 is explicitly narrower (“Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy”), introducing subtype mismatch risk for a generic DCM benchmark. On PRS-comparable evidence, both report similar PRS-only AUCs, but PGS004951 is slightly higher (0.67 vs 0.66) and shows stronger PRS effect sizes (OR 1.93 vs 1.73; β 0.66 vs 0.55), consistent with better standalone PRS signal. Although PGS004947 has a much larger validation sample (96,016 vs 7,761), validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the combination of better phenotype alignment plus stronger PRS-only/effect-size signals in PGS004951.

Both candidates are from the same Nat Med paper, use the same method (LDpred2), target the same CAD endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all match), have similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), and the same validation sample size, so the decision hinges on comparative support signals. PGS003725 shows materially stronger reported effect sizes (HR 1.75 and OR 2.14 per SD) than PGS003727 (HR 1.67 only), suggesting better PRS discrimination in the selected validation context. Structurally, PGS003725 also uses more variants (1,296,172 vs 1,125,113), a mild within-method advantage. Although PGS003727 has a simpler/cleaner-looking training cohort list (CARDIoGRAMplusC4D, UKB), PGS003725’s broader multi-cohort development plus stronger effect-size evidence makes it more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks given both lack PRS-only AUC/R2.

PGS004254 is the better-supported Crohn’s disease PRS because its endpoint is a direct Crohn’s disease diagnosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both Crohn’s disease) and it is built with a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) using a very large variant set (744,682), which is structurally favored for polygenic disease risk over sparse framework scores. Although PGS004254 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (its AUROC=0.72 is full-model and not directly comparable), it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=2.18), which is meaningful evidence of PRS discrimination. In contrast, PGS001330 comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank sparse framework (“across 813 traits”, snpnet) with only 220 variants and a time-to-event phenotype; despite having clean PRS-only metrics, they are weak (PGS-only AUROC≈0.576, R²≈0.0062), suggesting limited standalone PRS signal. Overall, the combination of stronger disease-focused evidence and stronger implied PRS signal favors PGS004254 over the weaker sparse framework score PGS001330.

Both candidates are near-clone PRS-CS genome-wide scores from the same Nat Genet study with the same mapped trait (dilated cardiomyopathy) and similar PRS-only discrimination/effect sizes (PGS-only AUC 0.68 vs 0.67; OR per SD 1.91 vs 1.93). PGS004949 is better supported for the target because its phenotyping_reported is more endpoint-faithful to dilated cardiomyopathy as a disease entity (“Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy”) than PGS004951’s broader/less specific “Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy,” and it is evaluated in the MAE ancestry (matching its GWAS mix and offering a clearer non-EUR transport context) with a much larger validation sample (326,106 vs 7,761). While PGS004951 has slightly higher delta R2 (0.101 vs 0.095) and more variants, these are small within-family differences and don’t outweigh PGS004949’s slightly better PRS-only AUC plus stronger validation breadth/scale and clearer phenotype definition.

Both candidates align well to the target (diverticular disease) and are UKB EUR-developed, but PGS000997 has substantially stronger directly comparable PRS evidence: it reports PRS-only AUROC=0.591 and PRS-only R2=0.0178 (no covariates) with basic covariates listed and multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS). PGS004544 has an exact ICD10 K57 endpoint and a moderate OR=1.32, but provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and comes from a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framing with unknown covariates, making its standalone PRS strength and comparability less supported on the visible fields. Given the benchmark goal and the lack of comparable metrics for PGS004544, PGS000997 is better-supported despite being from a pan-trait framework paper.

Both candidates are near-clone scores from the same Nat Genet study, same reported trait (Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)), same EFO mapping, same phenotyping_reported (Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy), and same method (PRS-CS), so endpoint fidelity and study archetype do not differentiate them. The main differentiators are PRS-only performance and effect sizes: PGS004949 reports higher univariate (PRS-only) AUC (0.68, CI 0.66–0.69) vs PGS004947 (0.66, CI 0.63–0.68) and stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.91; β 0.65) vs (OR 1.73; β 0.55), which are the most directly comparable signals of PRS strength here. Although PGS004947 has slightly more variants and a higher full-model liability R2, those are weaker/less comparable than the PRS-only AUC and OR, and its evaluation N is smaller. Therefore PGS004949 is better-supported as the likely stronger standalone PRS for dilated cardiomyopathy.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to Dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and consistent phenotyping_reported). PGS001254 has clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.6646; PGS R2 0.0247) but comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely small variant set (11, snpnet), a pattern that often generalizes poorly. PGS002092, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large genome-wide coverage (~484k variants) and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), which is stronger transportability evidence than EUR-only evaluation. Given the framework-penalty and sparsity concerns for PGS001254, PGS002092 is better-supported as the more likely to rank higher externally despite missing directly comparable AUC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), and evaluation context (same multi-ancestry eval string; same validation n=18,971) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. The only differentiators are method/structure and the selected validation partial correlation: PGS002092 uses genome-wide shrinkage (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (484,484 vs 2,443), which is a positive structural signal when metrics are otherwise missing, and it also has a slightly higher partial-r (0.0797 vs 0.0783). Given the framework-paper setting is identical for both, PGS002092 is better-supported on structural grounds while PGS001880 offers no compensating performance or design advantage.

Both candidates match the target trait well (all report all-cause dementia; PGS005170 is explicitly incident all-cause dementia, PGS004284 is all-cause dementia). Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS004284 (0.819 vs 0.761) is not a reliable cross-model discriminator, especially since covariate sets differ and full-model AUROC is often covariate-driven. PGS005170 has stronger structural and transportability support: it is an ensemble/integrative PRS combining 24 component PRSs with genome-wide scale (1,320,229 variants) and shows multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR), plus it reports a PRS-associated effect size (HR 1.25). In contrast, PGS004284 is a very sparse 50-variant score developed/evaluated only in UKB Europeans with no effect-size evidence shown. Given domain guidance favoring disease-focused, externally oriented, multi-ancestry/robust designs and multi-score aggregation when PRS-only metrics are absent, PGS005170 is better-supported for likely external benchmark performance.

PGS004614 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (diverticular disease) because it comes from a disease-focused diverticular-disease GWAS study and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (SBayesR) with very broad genome coverage (1,082,282 variants), which is structurally favored for polygenic traits and typically transfers better than sparse framework scores. It also shows multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/SAS) consistent with an externally oriented validation context. In contrast, PGS000997 is a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) using a sparse snpnet model (5,757 variants), a study archetype that domain guidance flags as systematically underperforming disease-focused models in external validation. Although PGS000997 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.591, R2 0.0178) and these are heritability-plausible, its endpoint is time-to-event (TTE) and its modest PRS-only performance plus framework origin make it less likely to rank highest than the disease-specific, genome-wide PGS004614 (whose reported AUROC is full-model and covariate-inflated by family history, so it is not used as the main advantage).

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication/family, same mapped trait (follicular lymphoma) and phenotyping_reported (“Nodular lymphoma”), identical EUR-only ancestry context, same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sample sizes, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC differences are weak evidence). With comparable covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), PGS000644 shows slightly better overall discrimination metrics (full-model AUROC 0.538 vs 0.532; pseudo-R² 0.00349 vs 0.00282) and a marginally higher per-SD OR (1.149 vs 1.133), while PGS000643’s higher top-1% OR is offset by weaker overall metrics and wide CIs. Given the minimal separations and non-PRS-only metrics, the edge to PGS000644 is slight.

PGS000644 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for follicular lymphoma because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant coverage (2,209,179) and reports PRS effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.149, CI 1.021–1.294) with clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Although its reported AUROC (0.538) is only a full-model metric and modest, PGS002304 also lacks PRS-only metrics and provides no effect sizes, while being an extremely sparse 6-variant GWAS-hits score with unknown covariates—making its higher full-model AUROC (0.61) hard to interpret as PRS signal. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (PGS000644 ‘nodular lymphoma’ maps to follicular lymphoma; PGS002304 is exact), so the structural PRS strength and cleaner covariate transparency favor PGS000644.

PGS001792 is better-supported for the glaucoma target because it has tighter endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are specifically Primary open-angle glaucoma, a well-defined glaucoma subtype) and it reports a clean PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / pgs_only_r2=0.03209), which is interpretable and below the glaucoma heritability ceiling provided. It is also developed across multiple biobanks (BBJ, BioMe, TWB, UCLA), which is more consistent with externally oriented, multi-cohort construction than a single-cohort portability framework. In contrast, PGS002043 comes from a UKB portability-style paper (single-cohort DEV=EUR only) with a generic glaucoma phenotype and provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0458) rather than a directly comparable PRS-only R2/AUC, making its performance evidence less directly actionable for ranking despite having multi-ancestry evaluation records.

Both candidates target primary open-angle glaucoma, but PGS001792 has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.03209 (and AUROC listed is full-model), which is directly interpretable for PRS strength, whereas PGS004944 reports only a full-model AUROC=0.748 with no PGS-only AUC/R2, making its discrimination largely non-comparable. PGS004944 does have a strong OR per SD (1.74) and very large validation n, but its phenotype is explicitly self-reported and its key metric is covariate-influenced; by contrast PGS001792 keeps endpoint fidelity (POAG) without the self-report qualifier and provides the more benchmark-relevant PRS-only metric support.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and diagnosis-like phenotyping). However, PGS001254 comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse-PRS framework ("across 813 traits") with an extremely sparse 11-variant model, which is a warning pattern for weaker external generalization despite reporting clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646; R2 0.0247). PGS001880, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, is a much less sparse penalized-regression score with far broader variant coverage (2443 variants) and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger transportability evidence than PGS001254’s EUR-only evaluation. Given the framework+sparsity penalty on PGS001254 and the broader, more portable design signals in PGS001880, PGS001880 is better-supported overall.

The two candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (good alignment to heart failure), same EFO mapping, same method (LDpred), identical variant count, ancestry distribution, covariates (age/sex/20 PCs), training cohort (MVP), and validation sample size. PGS004944 is better supported for the target trait glaucoma because it has higher endpoint fidelity (explicit Primary open-angle glaucoma with matching EFO open-angle glaucoma and phenotyping_reported as POAG self-report) and provides stronger PRS signal evidence via an effect size (OR per SD 1.74, a strong discriminative indicator) plus a reported AUROC (though full-model) with only basic covariates (age/age^2/sex/ancestry). Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported: lymphocytic thyroiditis/Hashimoto’s thyroiditis), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry string (MAE 100%), same validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), study context (same publication, UKB training n=6,704), ancestry distribution (DEV EUR; EVAL EUR+SAS), covariates (0), and validation size (n=90,274). PGS002763 is the better-supported match for the target trait hip osteoarthritis because its endpoint fidelity is direct (phenotyping_reported = "Hip osteoarthritis"), whereas PGS002728 uses a treatment/proxy endpoint (phenotyping_reported = "Total hip replacement"), which can introduce selection/indication effects beyond disease status.
