Overall, the cleaner disease endpoint plus stronger polygenic construction outweigh PGS002728’s multi-cohort development list and full-model AUROC.

PGS000643 is better-supported structurally for a follicular lymphoma target: its endpoint is effectively aligned (trait_efo=follicular lymphoma; phenotyping_reported “Nodular lymphoma” is a near-synonym for follicular/nodular NHL) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1,048,780 variants, which is generally more capable of capturing polygenic signal than PGS002304’s 6 genome-wide-significant-variant score. Overall, the stronger method/variant coverage plus cleaner covariate disclosure outweighs the modest full-model AUROC advantage of the sparse 6-SNP model.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (Hypertension; prevalent hypertension), come from the same Nat Commun paper, use the same covariates (age/sex/PCs plus smoking and BMI), and have essentially identical full-model AUROC (0.764 for PGS004236 vs 0.763 for PGS004234), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so metrics don’t meaningfully differentiate. Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), study context (same publication, UKB training n=6,704), covariates (0), ancestry distribution (DEV EUR; EVAL EUR+SAS), and validation size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R²). With endpoints and covariates matched, these advantages favor PGS004047.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo: Hodgkins lymphoma), come from the same publication and cohort context (MGI; EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL; same covariates age/sex/batch/PCs; same training n=736 and validation n=775), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics to separate them. Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (good match to heart failure), same EFO, same publication/cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same validation size (n=31,804) and ancestry distribution, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). Both candidates are near-clones: identical endpoint fidelity to heart failure (same PheCode 428.1 CHF NOS; same EFO), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distributions, same validation size (n=31,804), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). These gaps are tiny, so confidence is low, but they favor PGS005083.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (trait_efo) with identical reported/phenotyping labels (“lymphocytic thyroiditis”), same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix, and same validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is discounted for PRS ranking). Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), study context (same publication, UKB training n=6,704), covariates (0), ancestry distribution (DEV EUR; EVAL EUR+SAS), and validation size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not ideal for PRS comparison). PGS002728 has stronger endpoint fidelity to hip osteoarthritis as a clinically severe, clearly OA-related outcome (phenotyping_reported: total hip replacement) and comes from a disease-focused OA risk assessment study with multi-cohort development (EB, GARP, HUNT, LLS, MyCode, UKB, arcOGEN, deCODE) and basic covariates (age, sex), reducing concerns about packaged risk-factor integration. Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to Hodgkin’s disease/lymphoma with identical ancestry (EUR-only), cohorts (MGI), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and the same training (n=736) and validation size (n=775), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given this near-clone setting, the better-supported choice is the one with stronger observed validation performance: PGS000638 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0193 vs 0.013) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.377 vs 1.30) than PGS000637. PGS000637’s more complex PRS-CS genome-wide construction and larger variant count do not outweigh its weaker empirical performance within the same study/endpoint context.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target via trait_efo = osteoarthritis, hip and both are EUR-only evaluations with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so we fall back to endpoint fidelity + effect-size evidence and study archetype signals. PGS002763 has the most direct phenotype labeling (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both explicitly “Hip osteoarthritis”) and reports a stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.38, CI 1.31–1.46) than PGS004478 (OR≈1.296 with no CI shown), which is meaningful given effect sizes are the only comparable performance signal available. PGS004478 has a larger stated training sample (n=174,489) and slightly larger validation n, but training size is a weak differentiator here, and its publication framing (“Integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”) plus unknown covariates raises mild concern about risk-factor packaging/less transparent modeling compared with PGS002763’s explicitly basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical).

Both candidates target the same endpoint (Graves' disease; phenotyping_reported identical) and come from the same multi-cohort study with the same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). Given this near-clone context, PGS005265 is better-supported because it shows materially stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 1.625 vs 1.008 for PGS005264) and slightly higher reported AUROC (0.665 vs 0.659), and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far broader variant coverage (1,085,173 vs 112), which is structurally more consistent with capturing polygenic signal than the very sparse P+T score in PGS005264.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target hyperthyroidism via the clinically dominant subtype Graves’ disease: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, same method (PRSCS), essentially identical variant count (~1.085M), same evaluation ancestry mix and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), with covariates unknown for both and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). With endpoints and study context indistinguishable, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size differences: PGS005265 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6652 vs 0.6637) and stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.625 vs 1.543; β 0.486 vs 0.434), so it is marginally better supported. The gap is small, hence low confidence.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for the target (trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), come from the same publication, and have the same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size, so phenotype and transportability do not differentiate. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; the only AUROC shown is full-model and thus not a reliable cross-model discriminator, and the small full-model AUROC edge for PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.630) is likely noise given unknown covariates. The stronger differentiators are structural and effect-size evidence: PGS005271 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.55) than PGS005270’s very weak OR≈1.04 from a sparse P+T 55-variant score, making PGS005271 better-supported as a standalone PRS for external performance.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target trait (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), same phenotyping_reported, same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), same development cohorts, same validation sample size, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given this, the best available differentiators are the reported effect sizes and full-model metrics under identical covariates: PGS004911 shows consistently stronger signals than PGS004910 (AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; R² 0.048 vs 0.031; HR 2.34 vs 1.97; OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5). Additionally, PGS004911 is the MTAG-enhanced variant, which domain guidance mildly prefers over the non-MTAG sibling when endpoints are otherwise aligned. Therefore PGS004911 is better-supported.

Both candidates match the target trait (hypertension) at the concept level, but PGS004234 is from a disease-focused, hypertension-specific multi-ethnic study with explicit multi-ancestry development and evaluation (DEV includes AFR/AMR/EUR/ASN; EVAL is MAE), which is a positive transportability signal for a generic hypertension benchmark. In contrast, PGS001320 comes from the known pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as systematically underperforming disease-focused models in external validation despite clean metadata. While PGS001320 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.629, PGS-only R2 0.0649) and these are below the hypertension heritability ceiling (so plausible), its evidence is primarily single-biobank framework-derived and selected validation ancestry is European. PGS004234 lacks PRS-only metrics (only a full-model AUROC 0.763 with additional epidemiologic covariates like BMI/smoking), so its performance is less directly comparable, but the study archetype and multi-ancestry design make it more likely to transfer well than the framework sparse UKB score.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin's disease, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same cohorts/covariates, same training n=736 and validation n=775, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2). With PRS-comparable metrics absent for both, the best differentiator is the within-study empirical performance: PGS000639 shows stronger discrimination/effect evidence than PGS000637 (full-model AUROC 0.62 vs 0.574; Nagelkerke R² 0.0276 vs 0.013; OR per SD 1.476 vs 1.3; top 1% OR 2.64 vs 1.67). Given identical covariates, these gaps favor PGS000639, while PGS000637’s method/variant-count advantage (PRS-CS, 1,047,511 variants vs P+T, 20 variants) is outweighed here by the weaker observed validation metrics in the same setting.

PGS002653 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for hypothyroidism because it reports a PRS-relevant quantitative metric (incremental R2=0.0262) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, whereas PGS005218 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.859) that is likely dominated by heavy near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making its discrimination non-comparable to PRS performance. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (hypothyroidism), but PGS005218’s “incident hypothyroidism” plus biomarker-adjusted modeling looks more like clinical prediction packaging than pure genetic risk, while PGS002653’s setup is cleaner despite smaller validation and a framework-style publication context.

PGS004910 is better-supported as a standalone HCM PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (374,190) and reports PRS-relevant effect sizes (HR 1.97; OR 1.26 per SD; plus OR 5.5 high vs median tertile) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), reducing concern that performance is driven by clinical-risk packaging. In contrast, PGS000739 is a very sparse 27-variant GWAS-hits score and its reported AUROC=0.821 is from a covariate-heavy model including multiple clinical risk factors and rare-variant carrier status, making the full-model AUROC largely non-comparable to PRS-only performance and raising leakage/packaging concerns. Both match the endpoint (HCM) and are Nat Genet, but the cleaner covariate context and more polygenic construction favor PGS004910 for likely external PRS performance.

PGS004236 is from a disease-focused, multi-cohort, explicitly multi-ethnic hypertension study (BioMe/MVP/UKB) with broad evaluation ancestries and a strong reported PRS effect size (OR=2.1 per SD), which is supportive of real PRS discrimination even though it lacks a clean PGS-only AUROC/R2 (its reported AUROC=0.764 is full-model and covariate-influenced, including BMI/smoking). PGS001320 provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.629, R2=0.0649) and basic covariates, but it is a classic pan-trait UKB framework score (“across 813 traits”, snpnet) that domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable in external validation than disease-focused multi-cohort models unless it has clearly superior endpoint/metric evidence. With both having acceptable endpoint alignment to hypertension, the framework penalty plus PGS004236’s strong OR and multi-ancestry disease-focused design outweigh PGS001320’s modest PRS-only AUROC/R2 advantage.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypothyroidism) and both are UKB-based, but PGS004935 has more direct PRS signal evidence via a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.5, 95% CI 1.41–1.6), which domain guidance treats as meaningful discrimination support when PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. In contrast, PGS002653 reports only an incremental R2=0.0262 explicitly tied to a combined full model (BOLT-LMM + covariates), which is less directly comparable to standalone PRS performance and provides weaker isolated PRS evidence. While PGS002653 has broader evaluation ancestry and many more variants, the lack of a clean PRS-only metric and absence of effect-size support makes it less well-supported than PGS004935 on the visible fields.

PGS004911 is better-supported as a standalone HCM PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (374,114 vs 27 for PGS000739), and reports PRS-linked effect sizes (HR 2.34; OR per SD 1.33; plus high-vs-median-tertile OR 5.9) under only basic demographic/PC covariates, which is more comparable to PRS performance. Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), but PGS000739’s reported AUROC (0.821) is from a much more clinically augmented model (multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status), making its full-model discrimination less informative about PRS strength; it also relies on a sparse genome-wide-significant SNP set. Neither provides clean PGS-only AUC/R2, so structural/method and covariate comparability favor PGS004911.

Both candidates target Graves’ disease (a strong match to the broader hyperthyroidism target) with identical phenotyping_reported, evaluation ancestry (MAE), and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not directly comparable as PRS performance). Given this near-clone context, PGS005266 is better-supported because it shows materially stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 1.54, β=0.434) versus PGS005264’s essentially null effect (OR 1.008, β=0.008), and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far broader variant coverage (1,085,170 variants; PRSCS) compared with PGS005264’s sparse P+T score (112 variants). The small full-model AUROC difference (0.664 vs 0.659) is minor and not decisive, but it is directionally consistent with PGS005266.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (n=19,883), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. The main differentiators are (i) slightly stronger PRS-comparable performance signal: PGS002031 has higher partial correlation (0.1355 vs 0.1307), and (ii) stronger structural properties for a polygenic disease: PGS002031 uses genome-wide shrinkage (LDpred2) with many more variants (6,713 vs 654), which is generally favored over sparse penalized regression when other fields are equal. Given the small metric gap, confidence is moderate rather than high.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have similar EUR-only development/evaluation, identical basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and lack PRS-only AUC/R2—so endpoint subtype differences don’t clearly favor either for the broad target “juvenile idiopathic arthritis.” Given otherwise near-clone metadata, PGS000325 has stronger visible performance/effect evidence in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.80 vs 0.76; OR 1.93 vs 1.51), and also a larger variant set (21 vs 12), making it the better-supported choice than PGS000326.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to the umbrella JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly for the oligoarticular JIA subtype (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported), creating an endpoint-specificity mismatch for a generic JIA target. Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have similar basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and lack PRS-only AUC/R2; thus PGS000325’s higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.738) is not decisive and may reflect subtype separability rather than stronger general JIA PRS performance. Given comparable study archetype/ancestry context, endpoint fidelity favors PGS000114.

PGS004908 is better-supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it comes from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis and shows materially stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR=1.5 per SD) with a much larger variant set (107 vs 19). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the similar full-model AUROC values (0.74 for PGS004908 vs 0.722 for PGS000076) are not decisive and are influenced by covariates in both. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (PGS004908: kidney cancer/renal carcinoma; PGS000076: renal cell carcinoma/incident kidney cancer), but PGS000076 is from a cross-cancer evaluation with weaker per-SD association (HR=1.16), suggesting a weaker standalone PRS. Overall, PGS004908 has the stronger disease-focused evidence package and discriminative signal.

PGS004908 is the better-supported kidney cancer PRS: it is from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) with a substantially larger GWAS-hits set (107 variants) and shows a much stronger PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.5, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) than PGS000787 (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.07–1.24), which suggests materially stronger standalone genetic discrimination. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so their similar full-model AUROCs (0.74 vs 0.722) are not decisive and are influenced by comparable epidemiologic covariates; however, PGS000787 comes from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration framework and is explicitly derived from an older 19-variant score with inverse weights, which is weaker structural evidence than the direct disease GWAS-hits construction in PGS004908. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (renal carcinoma / renal cell carcinoma as dominant kidney cancer subtype), leaving the stronger effect-size and disease-focused study context to favor PGS004908.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same N18 chronic renal failure phenotype mapped to kidney failure), ancestry (EUR dev/eval), cohorts (UKB), variant count (~1.06M), training (n=174,489) and validation size (n=56,192), and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2. With metrics absent, the main differentiator is the available PRS effect size: PGS004562 reports a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.395) than PGS004492 (1.171), which is supportive of better standalone PRS discrimination. Although PGS004492 uses LDpred2 (a strong shrinkage method), within the same publication/endpoint context the stronger observed effect size in PGS004562 is the better-supported signal here.

PGS004492 has better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is N18 (Chronic renal failure), aligning with the generic kidney failure target, whereas PGS000708 is explicitly phenotyped as “Diabetic kidney failure in all,” a restricted subtype that is a mismatch for generic kidney failure risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS000708’s full-model C-index=0.779 (with age/sex/PCs) is not a comparable PRS metric and cannot outweigh the subtype mismatch. With metrics largely non-comparable, the more endpoint-faithful, genome-wide LDpred2 score with much larger variant coverage (1,059,939 vs 183,272) and similar moderate per-SD effect size evidence (OR~1.17 vs HR~1.19) is the better-supported choice.

PGS000114 is the better-supported choice for the target trait juvenile idiopathic arthritis because its endpoint fidelity is an exact match at all key fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all JIA), whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with a different EFO and phenotyping_reported, making it less directly aligned to the umbrella target. Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have EUR-only development/evaluation, and report only full-model AUROC (not PRS-only), so the small AUROC difference (0.76 vs 0.738) is not a reliable differentiator. With comparable covariates (sex, PCs) and no PRS-only metrics, PGS000114’s stronger effect-size evidence (OR 2.085 vs 1.51) and broader target-consistent phenotype outweigh PGS000326’s larger validation N and slightly higher full-model AUROC.

PGS005218 is better-supported for hypothyroidism because it comes from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with a much stronger structural PRS build (PRS-CS, genome-wide shrinkage; 1,110,091 variants) and broad multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.), whereas PGS004935 is from a portability/framework-style paper with a sparse SnpNet score (6,127 variants) trained only in UKB—an archetype that often generalizes worse. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable PRS metrics; moreover PGS005218’s very high AUROC (0.859) is paired with explicit near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) suggesting covariate inflation, but PGS004935’s AUROC=0.7 is also only a full-model metric with unknown covariates. With PRS-comparable metrics absent for both, the more disease-specific, genome-wide, multi-cohort score (PGS005218) is the more reliable pick despite the covariate-leakage concern.

PGS004562 is better aligned to the target trait as a general kidney failure/renal failure endpoint (phenotyping_reported: N18 chronic renal failure; trait_efo: kidney failure), whereas PGS000708 is explicitly restricted to a subtype/population (“Diabetic kidney failure in all”), which is a meaningful endpoint mismatch for generic “kidney failure” deployment. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural/effect-size evidence: PGS004562 reports a stronger per-SD effect (OR=1.395) than PGS000708 (HR=1.19), and uses a much larger genome-wide variant set (1,059,939 vs 183,272), consistent with capturing more polygenic signal. PGS000708’s reported C-index=0.779 is full-model (with age/sex/PCs) and not comparable as PRS performance, so it doesn’t outweigh the subtype mismatch and weaker effect size.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same ICD-10 M17 gonarthrosis; trait_efo osteoarthritis, knee), ancestry (EUR dev/eval), cohorts (UKB), training (n=174,489) and validation size (n=56,192), and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2. With metrics absent, the main differentiators are structural method signals and effect size: PGS004549 uses an explicit meta/ensemble-style approach (RFDiseasemetaPRS; multi-score aggregation is a positive structural signal) and shows a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.3667) than PGS004479 (LDpred2; OR 1.3233). Given otherwise identical context, the aggregation method plus higher OR makes PGS004549 better-supported.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease) and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R². PGS000054 has stronger PRS-specific evidence via an effect size (OR=1.73 per SD, suggesting strong discrimination) and uses only basic covariates (age, sex), with a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort development context and external evaluation in an AMR (Hispanic/Latin American) cohort. PGS000334 provides only a full-model/unspecified R²=0.191 from a C+T score with unknown covariates, which is not PRS-comparable and is also suspiciously high relative to the provided EUR heritability ceiling context, reducing trust in that metric. Given better interpretable PRS signal and cleaner covariate transparency, PGS000054 is better-supported.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (incident kidney cancer; EFO renal cell carcinoma), use the same 19-variant GWAS-hits construction, have identical ancestry context (EUR GWAS/EVAL), identical covariates, identical validation sample size (n=391,610), and essentially identical full-model discrimination/effect size (AUROC ~0.722; C-index ~0.723–0.724; HR per SD ~1.15–1.16). Candidate_b (PGS000787) is explicitly derived from candidate_a with inverse weights, and its reported R²=0.366 appears to be a full-model/other metric (not PRS-only) and is also implausibly above the provided kidney-cancer heritability ceiling (h2_liability ~0.0178), making it non-comparable/suspect for PRS ranking. With no clean PRS-only AUC/R² for either, the safer, better-supported choice is the original score (PGS000076) rather than an inverted-weight derivative.

Both candidates align well to the target (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R². PGS000053 is better-supported on the visible fields because it comes from a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort context (many AD cohorts listed) with clean/basic covariates (age, sex) and provides a PRS-relevant effect size (OR=1.29 per SD), giving at least some direct evidence of discriminative signal. PGS000334 reports only a generic R²=0.191 that appears to be full-model/unspecified (not PRS-only) with covariates listed as unknown, making the metric hard to interpret and potentially non-comparable; its training context is narrower (IGAP, UKB) and it provides no effect-size support. Given the lack of clean PRS-only metrics in both, the stronger endpoint-supporting study context plus interpretable effect-size evidence favors PGS000053.

Both candidates map cleanly to knee osteoarthritis (same trait_efo) and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we fall back to endpoint fidelity and PRS effect-size evidence. PGS002767 has a direct, unambiguous phenotype label (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Knee osteoarthritis”) and discloses a basic covariate set (age, sex, PCs, technical), reducing comparability concerns. PGS004479 uses an ICD-style label (“M17 Gonarthrosis”) which is still aligned but slightly less direct, and its covariates are unknown, lowering confidence in how performance was assessed. Effect sizes are very similar (OR per SD ~1.35 for PGS002767 vs ~1.32 for PGS004479), and structural differences (method/variant count/training N/validation N) are not decisive here, so the cleaner endpoint/covariate transparency gives PGS002767 a narrow edge.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported AUROCs are full-model and not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Given that, structural signals and effect sizes matter more: PGS004860 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with ~1.14M variants and shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.33) than PGS000078 (HR=1.16), suggesting more PRS signal. PGS000078’s evaluation is much larger but its reported discrimination is heavily bundled with extensive non-genetic predictors (family history, detailed smoking variables/interactions, PM2.5), making its full-model AUROC less informative for PRS quality; PGS004860’s covariates are lighter (age/sex/BMI/smoking/PCs). Overall, PGS004860 is better-supported as a stronger standalone PRS for lung cancer.

PGS000754 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target trait: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Systemic lupus erythematosus,” whereas PGS002082 uses a broader/less specific endpoint (“Lupus (localized and systemic)”) from a UKB portability framework paper. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS000754’s reported AUROC=0.65 is a full-model metric and cannot be treated as a clean PRS-comparable advantage, but it is still more direct performance evidence than PGS002082’s very small partial-r (0.0212). PGS002082 does have broader multi-ancestry evaluation and known basic covariates, but given the framework-study penalty and weaker/less disease-specific endpoint, PGS000754 is marginally better-supported for lupus erythematosus overall.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint (Chronic lymphocytic leukemia; phenotyping_reported identical), same publication/family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes, same covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs), and identical full-model AUROC (0.696) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so performance comparability is limited. With metrics essentially tied, PGS000648 has a slight edge via marginally stronger supporting signals: higher Nagelkerke R² (0.102 vs 0.0973), higher top-1% OR (12.9 vs 11.3), slightly higher per-SD OR (2.124 vs 2.104), and a larger variant set (44 vs 32), consistent with a modestly stronger score within the same study context.

PGS000754 is better supported as a standalone SLE PRS for the generic target “lupus erythematosus” because its endpoint is the general disease (“phenotyping_reported: Systemic lupus erythematosus”) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant coverage (293,684), which is a positive structural signal for a polygenic disease. In contrast, PGS000328 is explicitly restricted to an early-onset subtype (“onset before age 20”), creating an endpoint mismatch for the generic target, and it is a sparse GWAS-hits score (57 variants). Although PGS000328 reports a higher AUROC (0.83 vs 0.65), both are full-model AUROCs with unknown covariates (no PRS-only metrics), so that difference is not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator; thus endpoint fidelity + method/coverage favor PGS000754.

Both candidates are near-clones: same late-onset AD endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo) and same phenotyping_reported (familial LOAD), same method (genome-wide significant variants) with the same 21 variants, same basic covariates (age, sex), and same disease-focused multi-cohort development context. Neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so performance must be inferred from effect sizes and context. PGS000054 shows a materially stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR=1.29, 1.21–1.37), which is a meaningful discriminator within an otherwise identical sibling pair. Although PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792) and ancestry-matched EUR evaluation, validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the much stronger OR signal; PGS000054’s AMR evaluation also provides some transportability evidence rather than a clear penalty. Therefore PGS000054 is better-supported as the stronger PRS.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to the target (lymphoid leukemia) with identical trait_reported/trait_efo (chronic lymphocytic leukemia) and identical phenotyping_reported and covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and both are EUR-only throughout from the same publication family—so phenotype and leakage signals do not differentiate them. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, the best available comparative evidence is the within-family performance/effect-size package: PGS000648 shows consistently stronger discrimination and risk separation than PGS000647 (higher full-model AUROC 0.696 vs 0.675; higher Nagelkerke R² 0.102 vs 0.0689; higher OR per SD 2.124 vs 1.874; much higher top-1% vs rest OR 12.9 vs 4.11). Although PGS000647 has larger training and validation sample sizes, those are weak tie-breakers here and do not outweigh the materially stronger effect-size and performance signals for PGS000648.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS000789’s evaluation is heavily packaged with non-genetic risk factors and interactions (family history, PM2.5, detailed smoking variables and interaction terms), making its very high full-model AUROC/R² largely covariate-driven and less informative about standalone PRS quality. PGS004860 uses a genome-wide LDpred2 score (1,143,554 variants) with a comparatively lighter covariate set (age/sex/BMI/smoking status/PCs) and shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.33 vs HR 1.17), which is more indicative of PRS signal when PRS-only metrics are absent. Despite PGS000789’s much larger validation sample, the covariate-heavy packaging and weaker PRS effect size make it less likely to rank higher on external PRS benchmarks than the genome-wide LDpred2 model.

PGS004606 is a disease-focused age-related macular degeneration score (IAMDGC; Nat Genet) with clean endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all AMD) and strong PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 1.76), using only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC=0.71, which is not PRS-comparable), its study archetype and strong OR support suggest better external performance than PGS001013, which comes from the pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse snpnet framework with only 53 variants and weak PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.553; R2 0.006) consistent with a low-signal, less transferable framework score despite reporting PRS-only metrics and multi-ancestry evaluation.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (age-related macular degeneration) with identical phenotyping_reported and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not directly comparable as PRS performance). Given this near-clone setup, the best differentiators are the available discrimination proxies: PGS004606 shows materially stronger reported performance in the selected European validation (full-model AUROC 0.71 vs 0.65) and a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.76 vs 1.48), which is a meaningful PRS-quality signal. PGS004607’s AFR-only GWAS ancestry with EUR evaluation also suggests a potential ancestry-mismatch/transportability disadvantage versus PGS004606’s EUR GWAS + EUR evaluation alignment. Variant count differences are small and not decisive here.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/efo and phenotyping_reported), method (GWAS Hits), variant count (32), ancestry (EUR-only), covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs), and publication family, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given that, the best differentiator is the strength of the reported association/discrimination in the selected validation: PGS000646 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.696 vs 0.675), higher pseudo-R² (0.0973 vs 0.0689), and notably stronger effect size signals (OR per SD 2.104 vs 1.874; top 1% vs rest OR 11.3 vs 4.11) than PGS000647. PGS000647 has larger training/validation sample sizes (UKB; n=2,833 train, n=2,758 eval vs MGI; n=730 train, n=756 eval), but validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the consistently stronger effect-size/performance evidence for PGS000646 within this same-study sibling comparison.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait (melanoma), same endpoint (incident invasive melanoma), same covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same publication and validation sample size (n=4,765), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R², which are not PRS-comparable). With endpoints and study context effectively identical, the only differentiators are small full-model metric differences (AUROC 0.691 vs 0.688; R² 0.072 vs 0.070—too small to be meaningful) and structural variant count, where PGS002247 includes more genome-wide significant variants (68 vs 50), a modest within-method advantage. Hence PGS002247 is slightly better-supported, but the evidence gap is minimal.

Although PGS004607 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (so confidence is not high), its disease-focused design and stronger structural/effect-size evidence outweigh the framework-score advantages of PGS001013.

Both candidates are near-clones: same myocardial infarction PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same method (LDpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported Lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer), identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical covariate-heavy evaluation (includes family history, PM2.5, detailed smoking terms), and essentially identical reported full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849) with similar HR per SD (1.16 vs 1.17). Candidate_b (PGS000789) is explicitly a derivative of candidate_a with inverse variant weights, which is a red flag for biological/PRS-direction coherence rather than a clear improvement, and its additional R²=0.799 appears to be a full-model/packaged metric (not PRS-only) and is implausibly high relative to the lung cancer heritability ceiling context, so it does not provide reliable PRS-strength evidence. Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to multiple myeloma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), use the same method (genome-wide significant variants) with the same variant count (23), and are EUR-only in GWAS and evaluation, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either record (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator). Validation size differences (2,395 vs 290) are weak signals but mildly favor PGS002281 as well.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to multiple myeloma; both EUR-only evaluation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative. Still, PGS002281 comes from a disease-focused multiple-myeloma PRS paper and shows stronger validation evidence on the visible record (full-model AUROC 0.644 with OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18) than PGS000653 (full-model AUROC 0.577; OR top 1% vs rest 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1). Methods/variant counts are near-identical (23 vs 22 GWAS-hit/GWS variants) and validation Ns are similar, so the stronger effect-size/discrimination signals favor PGS002281.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo and same phenotyping_reported string), method (PRSCS), evaluation ancestry (MAE 100%), and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported (MI PheCode 411.2), same trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (myocardial infarction), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), identical ancestry_distribution strings, same validation sample size (n=30,379) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index reported, which is not PRS-comparable). PGS002246 is better supported for the target trait melanoma because its endpoint is more explicitly aligned to generic melanoma risk in a disease-focused evaluation context (phenotyping_reported: “Incident invasive melanoma”; publication explicitly about independent evaluation of melanoma PRS in UK and Australian prospective cohorts). PGS003382, while closely related (skin cutaneous melanoma), comes from a cross-cancer study archetype (“across cancers”), which is a weaker signal for melanoma-specific PRS optimization unless it has clearly stronger PRS-comparable metrics—which it does not (both candidates only report full-model AUROC/R², no PGS-only metrics). With PRS-only metrics absent for both, the small full-model AUROC difference (0.688 vs 0.682) is essentially noise, and PGS002246’s cleaner, melanoma-centric endpoint framing outweighs PGS003382’s larger variant count and much larger validation N.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores, so phenotype fidelity does not separate them. PGS001270 has cleaner PRS-only metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.6586; PGS-only R2=0.0290) and these are plausible under the MS heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.117), but it comes from the sparse pan-trait snpnet “813 traits” framework with only 41 variants—an archetype that often generalizes worse. PGS002038, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (129,077) and is explicitly evaluated across more ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), which is a stronger structural/transportability signal than a very sparse pan-trait model’s modest PRS-only AUROC. Given the near-tie and missing comparable metrics for PGS002038, confidence is low, but the method/coverage advantage favors PGS002038.

PGS002082 is the better-supported choice for the broad target trait “lupus erythematosus” because its phenotype is aligned to lupus as an umbrella (“Lupus (localized and systemic)”), uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (361,553), and—critically—has explicit multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), supporting portability. Although it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, it at least reports a PRS-comparable partial correlation (partial-r=0.0212). In contrast, PGS000328 is narrower and endpoint-restricted (systemic lupus erythematosus, specifically onset before age 20), uses only 57 genome-wide significant variants, and its only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.83 with unknown covariates (not PRS-comparable and potentially covariate-driven), with evaluation limited to EUR only. Overall, PGS002082 has stronger structural properties and broader validation context, while PGS000328’s apparent metric advantage is not directly interpretable as PRS performance and is tied to a restricted early-onset endpoint.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple sclerosis). PGS002038 is from a UKB portability framework paper and only reports a weak PRS-comparable signal (partial-r=0.0396) with no AUC/R2/effect-size evidence, despite large training/validation; this archetype is explicitly penalized for external performance reliability. PGS002726 is disease-focused (IMSGC; Brain paper) and, while it lacks PRS-only metrics and reports only a full-model AUROC (0.80) that is not directly comparable, it also provides strong MS-specific risk stratification evidence (OR top 10% vs median = 15.0) and is not framed as a pan-trait portability score. Given framework-penalty vs disease-focused evidence, PGS002726 is better-supported to rank higher.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple sclerosis). However, PGS001270 is explicitly a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (41 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically underperforming disease-focused models in external validation despite having clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (PGS-only AUROC 0.6586; R2 0.0290, below the h2_liability ceiling). PGS002726 comes from a disease-focused MS study anchored on the IMSGC consortium and reports strong PRS discrimination evidence via effect size (OR top 10% vs median = 15.0) and a high AUROC (0.80) albeit only as a full-model metric with unknown covariates (so not directly comparable as PRS-only). Given the strong disease-focused archetype and much richer genome-wide variant inclusion (476,399 variants) versus the sparse framework score, PGS002726 is more likely to rank higher in an external benchmark for MS risk prediction, though confidence is tempered by the lack of explicit PRS-only AUC/R2 and unknown covariates.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Tobacco use disorder” mapped to nicotine dependence), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), and validation size (n=19,400) from the same portability paper—so performance evidence and structural signals dominate. PGS002037 shows stronger PRS signal in the selected record via higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.0741 vs 0.0557 for PGS001830) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (847,691 vs 13,838), which is generally favorable for polygenic traits when other fields are matched. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, these two advantages make PGS002037 better-supported than PGS001830.

Both candidates are near-clones: same obesity ICD10 E66 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication, same EUR-only training/evaluation (UKB; n=174,489 train; n=56,192 validation), same variant count, and no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported for either—so performance metrics cannot differentiate. The main visible differentiator is effect size: PGS004447 reports a higher OR per SD (1.36) than PGS004517 (1.23), which is supportive of stronger PRS discrimination given otherwise identical context. Method_name differs (LDpred2 vs RFDiseasemetaPRS), but within the same study family and without PRS-only metrics, the stronger reported OR is the more reliable tie-break here.

PGS004447 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target trait obesity: trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are explicitly ICD10 E66 (Obesity) with trait_efo=obesity, whereas PGS002033 uses a broader, less specific phenotype bundle (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”). Neither candidate reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so performance can’t be cleanly separated on discrimination metrics; however PGS004447 at least provides an OR per SD (~1.36), while PGS002033 only reports a modest partial correlation (partial-r ~0.079) that is harder to interpret for disease-risk ranking. Although PGS002033 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation (a portability-style paper) and known basic covariates, that framework/portability context plus the broader phenotype makes it less likely to be the best obesity-specific score than the more diagnosis-aligned PGS004447.

PGS004517 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target trait obesity: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly ICD10 E66 (Obesity) with trait_efo=obesity, whereas PGS002033 uses a broader administrative/bundle phenotype (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”) that is less specific to obesity alone. Neither candidate provides clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be compared directly; however PGS004517 at least reports an effect size (OR=1.22554), while PGS002033 only reports a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0789), which is harder to interpret for disease-risk discrimination. Although PGS002033 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation (a portability-style paper) and known basic covariates, that framework/portability context plus the broader phenotype makes it less likely to be the best obesity-specific score than the more endpoint-faithful, disease-coded PGS004517.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported is the same, despite spelling noise), come from the same publication family, have the same evaluation ancestry distribution (MAE 100%) and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so full-model AUROC differences (0.5876 vs 0.5854) are essentially non-decisive. Given that, structural and effect-size evidence favors PGS005263: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a materially stronger per-SD effect (OR 1.362; β 0.309) than PGS005261’s sparse P+T score with 110 variants and much weaker effect (OR 1.048; β 0.047). This combination makes PGS005263 better-supported as the more predictive standalone PRS for benign nodular goiter.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are identical: incident ovarian cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL; same covariates and validation N=211,958), and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2. Candidate_b (PGS000793) is explicitly a derivative of candidate_a (PGS000082) using the same 36 variants but with inverse weights, which is a red flag for biological/plausibility support rather than an independently optimized PRS. With no PRS-only metrics to justify that inversion, the safer, better-supported choice is the original disease PRS (PGS000082), despite candidate_b showing slightly higher full-model AUROC/HR that are not PRS-comparable and likely covariate-influenced.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to multiple myeloma; both EUR-only). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable as standalone PRS performance. Given that, PGS000653 is better-supported on visible PRS-relevant evidence: it provides basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4) and reports PRS-associated effect sizes (OR per SD 1.327) plus additional metrics (Nagelkerke R² 0.0145, Brier, top-1% OR), and it has explicit training/development context (UKB; samples_training n=3,377) with a larger evaluation sample (n=2,738). Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical typo) and come from the same study with identical ancestry distribution, cohort list, and validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS metric). Both candidates align to otosclerosis (trait_efo matches), but PGS001255 provides directly PRS-comparable performance evidence (PGS-only AUROC=0.6319 and PGS-only R2=0.01341) with basic covariates, and its PRS-only R2 is plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling sanity-check. PGS002768 is the better-supported osteoporosis PRS on endpoint fidelity and likely external performance: it targets a straightforward clinical osteoporosis phenotype (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Osteoporosis”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is structurally better aligned with a highly polygenic architecture than a very sparse model. Although PGS001274 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC ~0.576; R2 ~0.009) and multi-ancestry evaluation, those metrics are modest and the framework+sparse+TTE combination is a strong negative archetype; PGS002768 at least provides a moderate per-SD OR (1.31) on a direct endpoint with basic covariates, making it more likely to rank higher in an external benchmark for generic osteoporosis risk.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo = osteoarthritis, knee) and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we must lean on endpoint fidelity, study archetype, and structural signals. PGS004549 uses an ICD-style knee OA endpoint (M17 gonarthrosis) that is still a direct diagnosis match, and it is built as an aggregated/meta-PRS (RFDiseasemetaPRS), a structural positive signal versus the single-score PRS-CS approach in PGS002767. Overall, the meta-PRS construction plus slightly stronger effect size and clearer development support make PGS004549 more likely to rank higher.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper with identical training cohort (UKB), training N (269,704), covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size (24,905), so the decision rests on endpoint fidelity vs PRS-only performance. The time-to-event 'osteoporosis without pathological fracture' endpoint in candidate_a is a mild phenotype mismatch for a generic osteoporosis target, but not enough to outweigh its better PRS-only discrimination evidence given otherwise identical study context; both R2 values remain well below the heritability ceiling, so the metric edge is plausible.

PGS000082 has better endpoint fidelity for the broad target “ovarian neoplasm”: its phenotyping is a direct disease endpoint (“Incident ovarian cancer”), whereas PGS003394 is framed as “10-year ovarian cancer risks,” which is horizon-conditioned risk packaging and a negative signal for standalone PRS transfer. Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = pancreatic cancer/exocrine pancreatic carcinoma), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same cohorts (UKB), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs1-4), and same validation N (3,591), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either (only full-model metrics, which are not strongly comparable PRS evidence). Both candidates are from the same disease-focused Lancet Neurol PD GWAS meta-analysis, with identical reported phenotype (Parkinson’s disease), identical basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), identical training cohorts and training N, and the same validation sample size (n=999), so endpoint fidelity and study archetype do not differentiate them. Given otherwise near-clone metadata, the higher-coverage score with stronger effect-size support is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks.

PGS003586 is the better-supported match to the target trait preeclampsia: its trait_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia” and phenotyping_reported is “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia,” aligning cleanly with the endpoint, whereas PGS003587 is reported as “Gestational hypertension” despite sharing the same phenotyping string. Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are Osteoporosis for both), but PGS002768 is structurally more likely to generalize: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, whereas PGS001273 is a very sparse snpnet score (316 variants) from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” framework, which is a documented underperformer archetype in external validation. Net: stronger method/coverage and study archetype for PGS002768 outweigh the modest PRS-only metric advantage of PGS001273.

PGS000903 is better-supported as a standalone Parkinson’s disease PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis study family with explicit multi-cohort development (23andMe, IPDGC, UKB, etc.), uses a substantially richer polygenic model (1805 variants via C+T), and provides stronger PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25; beta reported) alongside basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). Neither reports clean PGS-only AUC/R2, so the decision rests on endpoint/study support and structural strength, favoring PGS000903.

PGS000793 has better endpoint fidelity to the generic target “ovarian neoplasm”: its phenotyping is a direct disease endpoint (“Incident ovarian cancer”), whereas PGS003394 is packaged as horizon-specific prediction (“10-year ovarian cancer risks”), which domain guidance flags as a risk-wrapper/absolute-risk formulation that is less comparable for standalone PRS ranking. PGS003394’s multi-ancestry evaluation is a plus, but its covariates are unknown and the horizon-packaging concern plus weaker available performance/effect-size evidence makes it less well-supported overall than PGS000793.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept (peripheral vascular disease) because its endpoint is a clear, clinically specific diagnosis—incident peripheral artery disease (PAD)—and it comes from a disease-focused PAD/MALE study with broad multi-cohort development and large, multi-ancestry evaluation (validation n=304,294 across AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS/AMR). Neither has PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint fidelity + disease-focused design + stronger effect-size evidence favors PGS005217.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; pancreatic cancer). Overall, the stronger effect size and broader evaluation support favor PGS000083 despite covariate comparability concerns.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and evaluation/ancestry distribution and validation N (n=19,668). Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (ICD10 J33 nasal polyp; same EFO), study context (same Commun Biol paper), ancestry (EUR dev/eval), training cohort (UKB), training N (174,489) and validation N (56,192), and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 so metrics cannot differentiate.
